summary.text: A 28-year-old multiparous patient was received 2 hours after a vaginal delivery of a newborn alive weighing 2750 grams in a peripheral maternity 3 km away and was referred for postpartum hemorrhage; the medical history was featureless. On admission there was hypovolemic shock with blood pressure 76/44 mmHg, regular tachycardia at 136 beats per minute and polypnea to 39 cycles per minute, and the obstetrical examination found an involuted uterus, endouterine fluid and red blood, and purpura.

A significant postpartum hemorrhage complicated by coagulopathy was concluded. Blood count at admission highlighted severe thrombocytopenia with 23,000 platelets and hemoglobin of 3.9 g/dl. Resuscitation measures were taken, and transfusion of 1120 ml whole blood, 350 ml red cell pellets and 860 ml fresh frozen plasma helped to manage coagulopathy and anemia; post natal care was also administered.

After seven days of hospitalization the patient was going after an amendment to the clinical symptoms and normal laboratory tests. Twenty five days later the patient returned to obstetric emergencies for significant bleeding with severe anemia (hemoglobin 9 g/dL) and without signs of hypovolemic shock. The gynecological examination, coagulation balance sheet and transvaginal Doppler ultrasound were reported normal; treatment was based on oxytocin, tranexamic acid, etamsylate and strict regular monitoring, and without arterial embolization the patient was going with ambulatory monitoring.

Two weeks later the patient presented again with rebleeding requiring hospitalization, resulting in a total hysterectomy after conditioning of the patient. Histological examination of the surgical specimen showed, in the cervix and uterine body, proliferation of arterial vessels of large and small caliber with tissue hemorrhage, and the retained diagnosis was a mixed form of cavernous hemangioma of the myometrium with localized capillary hemangioma of the cervix. The postoperative course was simple.

ambiguities.issue: The case text refers to the patient as "she" in four sentences but uses the possessive "His" once ("His medical history was featureless"), and the discussion prints "his admission". The repeated subject pronoun "she" is used for documented sex; the possessive slips are kept review_only as an ambiguity, not a conflict.
